text.p: The French government said on Friday it had halted the privatisation of Thomson-CSF and would propose an alternative solution to build a French defence electronics conglomerate based on the company.

The state will retain a stake that gives it ultimate decision-making power, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's office said in a statement issued after markets closed on the eve of a long Bastille Day holiday weekend.
New guidelines, aimed at promoting European defence industry cooperation, would be put into practice "in the coming weeks," it said.

Jospin's Socialist-led government suspended the process of selling the state's 58 percent holding in Thomson-CSF launched by its conservative predecessors after it won an upset victory in a parliamentary election on June 1.
Two French companies, the conglomerate Lagardere Groupe and engineering firm Alcatel Alsthom, had bid on the company and Britain's GEC-Marconi had also expressed interest.

Former prime minister Alain Juppe was forced to call off a first attempt to sell parent company Thomson SA to Lagardere privately last year after the state Privatisation Commission objected to the sale of its Thomson Multimedia (TMM) subsidiary to South Korea's Daewoo Group.
Alcatel had associated itself with state-owned plane maker Aerospatiale in its bid.

"The government has decided, in accordance with the applicable rules, to end the privatisation procedure under way for Thomson-CSF, which does not preserve the interests of the state, the company and its employees," the statement said.
"The government intends to define an industrial solution aimed at creating, with Thomson-CSF, a French professional and defence electronics pillar with a decisive public shareholding.
"This solution will be in the perspective of alliances destined to reinforce the European defence industry. These guidelines will be put into practice in the coming weeks."
The term "a decisive state shareholding" could mean anything from a controlling stake to a blocking minority or a golden share with decision-making rights on national security issues.
Alcatel said in a statement it was awaiting the new government decisions and remained interested in being a central part of alliances in the French defence industry.
There was no immediate reaction from Lagardere Groupe, a missiles-to-publishing empire which controls electronics firm Matra SA, which has now seen its second attempt to buy Thomson thwarted.
In May Lagardere chairman Jean-Luc Lagardere said an end to the selloff would be "rather serious" but "not tragic."
Thomson-CSF chairman Marcel Roulet said last week that his company risked being left behind in the restructuring of the European defence industry if the state kept majority control.
In testimony to the National Assembly defence committee, he said: "The capital structure of Thomson-CSF constitutes a handicap due to the majority held by the state."
Recent moves by GEC showed the strength and dynamism of private British defence groups which could undermine Thomson-CSF on the European scene, he added.
